subject: Fysik
title: The solar system and the seasons
sourceSummary: The structure of the solar system with the sun, rocky planets and gas giants, and how the Earth's rotation gives us day and night while the tilt of its axis gives us the seasons. You also practise the phases of the moon and the difference between a solar and a lunar eclipse.

questions.prompt: Which of these planets lies closest to the sun?
questions.opener: Go through the order of the planets from the inside out.
choices: Venus
Mercury
Mars
Jupiter
questions.explanation: Mercury is the innermost planet, followed by Venus, Earth and Mars. Venus is second closest — it's actually the hottest of all the planets, but that's because of its thick atmosphere, not because it's closest to the sun.

questions.prompt: Why do we have day and night on Earth?
questions.opener: Think about which movement takes roughly 24 hours.
choices: The Earth travels once around the sun in a day
The sun goes out during the night and switches back on in the morning
The moon blocks the sun every night
The Earth rotates once around its own axis in about 24 hours
questions.explanation: The Earth spins around its own axis in about 24 hours, and the half facing the sun has day while the half facing away has night. The Earth going round the sun instead takes a whole year, so that can't explain the daily cycle.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason we have seasons?
questions.opener: Look at how the Earth's axis is tilted relative to its orbit around the sun.
choices: The Earth's axis is tilted, so the hemispheres receive the sun's rays at different angles over the year
The Earth is much closer to the sun in summer than in winter
The sun shines more strongly during the summer half of the year
The moon blocks sunlight during winter
questions.explanation: The Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees, so during summer our hemisphere tilts towards the sun, the sun sits high in the sky and its rays hit more directly from above and for more hours each day. The distance to the sun only changes by a few per cent over the year — plus it's summer in the southern hemisphere at the same time as we have winter, which distance to the sun cannot explain.

questions.prompt: Why does the moon look different over the course of a month?
questions.opener: The sun always lights up exactly half the moon — but we see that half from different angles.
choices: The moon changes shape as it spins
The Earth's shadow falls on the moon every night
We see different amounts of the moon's sunlit half depending on where the moon is in its orbit
The moon shines with its own light, which varies in strength
questions.explanation: The moon doesn't shine on its own — it reflects sunlight, and the sun always lights up half of it. As the moon moves around the Earth, we see the lit half from different angles, which gives us the phases new moon, half moon and full moon. The Earth's shadow doesn't come into it — that only causes a lunar eclipse, which happens rarely.

questions.prompt: What happens during a solar eclipse?
questions.opener: Something gets in the way between you and the sun.
choices: The Earth ends up between the sun and the moon
The sun goes out for a short while
The Earth's shadow falls on the moon
The moon ends up between the sun and the Earth and shades part of the Earth
questions.explanation: During a solar eclipse the moon lines up directly between the sun and the Earth, and the moon's shadow falls on a narrow area of the Earth's surface where the sun is blocked out. The Earth ending up between the sun and the moon is instead a lunar eclipse, when the Earth's shadow covers the moon.

questions.prompt: Which four planets are the inner rocky planets?
questions.opener: The rocky planets are the four that lie closest to the sun.
choices: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars
Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune
Venus, Earth, Mars and Jupiter
Mercury, Earth, Saturn and Neptune
questions.explanation: The four innermost planets — Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars — are small and have a solid, rocky surface, which is why they're called rocky planets. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune lie beyond the asteroid belt and are instead large gas giants with no solid surface to land on.

questions.prompt: The moon's phase cycle, meaning the time from one new moon to the next, is about 29.5 days. How many days does it take from new moon to full moon?
questions.opener: Full moon occurs halfway through the cycle, i.e. after half the time.
steps: The order in the cycle is new moon, waxing half moon, full moon, waning half moon, then new moon again.
So the full moon falls exactly halfway through the cycle.
Split the cycle in two: 29.5 / 2 = 14.75 days.
So the answer is about 15 days, just over two weeks.
Sanity check: the half moon falls halfway there, about a week after new moon — just as we see in the sky.

questions.prompt: Summarise the solar system, the day-night cycle, the seasons and the moon.
questions.opener: Take the planets in order first, then the Earth's two movements, and finally the moon.
questions.answer: Solar system: the sun at the centre, eight planets in orbit around it, plus moons, asteroids and comets · Planet order from the inside: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune · Rocky planets: the four inner ones, small with a solid surface · Gas giants: the four outer ones, large with no solid surface · The sun is a star that shines with its own light, the planets reflect sunlight · Rotation: the Earth spins once around its own axis in about 24 hours, giving us day and night · Orbit: the Earth goes once around the sun in about 365 days, giving us the year · Seasons: the Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees, summer when our hemisphere tilts towards the sun (high sun, long days), winter when it tilts away · The northern and southern hemispheres have opposite seasons · Phases of the moon: new moon, waxing half moon, full moon, waning half moon, the whole cycle about 29.5 days · Solar eclipse: the moon between the sun and the Earth · Lunar eclipse: the Earth between the sun and the moon, the Earth's shadow on the moon

questions.prompt: Which planet is known for its clear rings?
questions.opener: The rings are made of ice and rock and are clearly visible even in a small telescope.
choices: Mars
Jupiter
Saturn
Mercury
questions.explanation: Saturn has the most famous and clearest ring system of all the planets in the solar system, made up of ice and rock fragments. Mars and Mercury have no visible rings.

questions.prompt: What are the four outer planets called that are large and have no solid surface?
questions.opener: These planets are mostly made of gas and have no ground to land on.
choices: Rocky planets
Gas giants
Dwarf planets
Asteroids
questions.explanation: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are called gas giants because they are large and are mostly made of gas with no solid surface. The rocky planets are instead the four small inner planets with a solid surface.

questions.prompt: A day on Earth is about 24 hours. What causes this?
questions.opener: Distinguish between the Earth's two different movements: one that takes a day and one that takes a year.
choices: The Earth's orbit around the sun
The Earth's rotation around its own axis
The moon's orbit around the Earth
The sun's rotation around its own axis
questions.explanation: The Earth's rotation around its own axis takes about 24 hours and gives us the day-night cycle. The Earth's orbit around the sun instead takes a whole year, so it can't explain the day.

questions.prompt: Which hemisphere has summer when the Earth's axis tilts towards the sun on that hemisphere?
questions.opener: Think about what applies to our own hemisphere in summer compared to the opposite hemisphere.
choices: Only the northern hemisphere, always
Only the southern hemisphere, always
The hemisphere that tilts towards the sun has summer, the other has winter
Both hemispheres have summer at the same time
questions.explanation: The hemisphere that is tilted towards the sun at that time gets the sun's rays more directly from above and has summer, while the opposite hemisphere tilts away and has winter. That's why the northern and southern hemispheres always have opposite seasons.

questions.prompt: What is the phase of the moon called when the whole sunlit half of the moon is visible from Earth?
questions.opener: This happens right in the middle of the moon's phase cycle.
choices: New moon
Half moon
Full moon
Lunar eclipse
questions.explanation: At full moon, we see the whole sunlit half of the moon, since the Earth is between the sun and the moon without shadowing it. At new moon, it's instead the far, dark half that faces us.

questions.prompt: The moon's phase cycle is about 29.5 days. How many days does it take from full moon to the next new moon?
questions.opener: The full moon sits in the middle of the cycle — how much of the cycle remains from there?
steps: The order in the cycle is new moon, waxing half moon, full moon, waning half moon, and then new moon again.
The full moon sits exactly halfway through the cycle, so half a cycle remains until the next new moon.
Divide the cycle in two: 29.5 / 2 = 14.75 days.
The answer is about 15 days, just over two weeks after the full moon.
Sanity check: this is the same length of time it took from new moon to full moon, since the full moon sits exactly in the middle of the cycle.

questions.prompt: During a lunar eclipse, where is the Earth?
questions.opener: Think about what shadows what during a lunar eclipse, compared to a solar eclipse.
choices: Between the sun and the moon, so the Earth's shadow falls on the moon
Behind the moon
Between the sun and another planet
The moon is between the sun and the Earth instead
questions.explanation: During a lunar eclipse, the Earth is between the sun and the moon, and the Earth's shadow falls on the moon. During a solar eclipse, it's instead the moon that is between the sun and the Earth.
